claim: Multicellularity has evolved more than 50 times across the tree of life.
source: Multicellularity has evolved more than 50 times across the tree of life (Umen and Herron, 2021; Grosberg and Strathmann, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Umen and Herron, 2021 and Grosberg and Strathmann, 2007

claim: Complex multicellularity has only evolved in lineages that develop clonally.
source: 'complex multicellularity' (Knoll, 2011; e.g. plants, animals, fungi, red algae and brown algae) has only evolved in lineages that develop clonally (Brunet and King, 2017; Knoll, 2011; Fisher et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Brunet and King, 2017; Knoll, 2011; Fisher et al., 2020

claim: Clonal development prevents intra-organism genetic conflict by limiting within-group genetic diversity.
source: By limiting within-group genetic diversity, clonal development prevents intra-organism genetic conflict, as there is little standing within-group genetic variation for selection to act on Buss, 2014; Maynard Smith and Szathmary, 1997; Clarke, 2014.
evidence: Supported by citations to Buss, 2014; Maynard Smith and Szathmary, 1997; Clarke, 2014

claim: Snowflake yeast were created by knocking out ACE2 in a unicellular ancestor.
source: We created clonal 'snowflake yeast' by knocking out ACE2 in a unicellular ancestor (Ratcliff et al., 2017; Pentz et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citations to Ratcliff et al., 2017; Pentz et al., 2020

claim: Aggregative floc yeast were created by placing the FLO1 gene under transcriptional control of the GAL1 promoter.
source: aggregative 'floc' yeast (GAL1p::FLO1 /GAL1p::FLO1)
evidence: Described in the abstract and methods sections

claim: Twenty replicate populations of both snowflake and floc yeast were evolved for 24 weeks.
source: We evolved 20 replicate populations of otherwise isogenic clonally reproducing 'snowflake' yeast (Δace2/∆ace2) and aggregative 'floc' yeast (GAL1p::FLO1 /GAL1p::FLO1) with daily selection for rapid growth in liquid media
evidence: Described in the abstract and experimental evolution methods

claim: Both snowflake yeast and floc evolved to settle significantly faster over 24 weeks.
source: Both snowflake yeast and floc evolved to settle significantly faster (one-way ANOVA; floc: F23,456=16.57, p<0.0001; snowflake: F23,456=13.65, p<0.0001, pairwise differences assessed with Tukey's post-hoc HSD with α=0.05).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Floc exhibited a 12-fold increase in settling rate after 24 weeks.
source: Floc, however, exhibited a much larger increase in settling rate than snowflake yeast (12-fold increase vs 1.3-fold increase after 24 weeks, respectively, Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1C

claim: Snowflake yeast exhibited a 1.3-fold increase in settling rate after 24 weeks.
source: Floc, however, exhibited a much larger increase in settling rate than snowflake yeast (12-fold increase vs 1.3-fold increase after 24 weeks, respectively, Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1C

claim: Evolved snowflake yeast increased their biomass weighted mean forward scatter by an average of 33%.
source: Biomass weighted mean forward scatter (a proxy for group size) increased by an average of 33% (Figure 2A and B; one-sided t-test, t=7.48, n=24, p<0.0001; non-overlayed histograms for individual snowflake isolates shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2A and B

claim: Thirteen floc populations showed significantly increased flocculation efficiency relative to the ancestor.
source: Thirteen populations showed significantly increased flocculation efficiency relative to the ancestor (one-way ANOVA, F(20,46)=45.53, p<0.0001, pairwise differences assessed with Tukey's honestly significant difference [HSD] with ɑ=0.05).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Floc yeast showed a 15% average fitness increase over their ancestor.
source: Floc yeast showed a significantly higher increase in fitness than snowflake yeast, increasing by an average of 15% as opposed to 7%, respectively (Figure 3A first panel: one-sample t-test, n=20, p<0.0001).
evidence: Supported by competition experiments shown in Figure 3A

claim: Snowflake yeast showed a 7% average fitness increase over their ancestor.
source: Floc yeast showed a significantly higher increase in fitness than snowflake yeast, increasing by an average of 15% as opposed to 7%, respectively (Figure 3A first panel: one-sample t-test, n=20, p<0.0001).
evidence: Supported by competition experiments shown in Figure 3A

claim: Floc yeast showed a 24% fitness advantage during growth.
source: Floc yeast showed a significant fitness advantage during growth (Figure 3A; mean increase = 24%, one-sample t-test, n=20 t=10.55, p<0.0001)
evidence: Supported by competition experiments shown in Figure 3A

claim: Floc yeast showed only a 3% fitness advantage during settling selection, which was not statistically significant.
source: but despite settling an average of 12-fold faster than their ancestor when grown in monoculture, were only slightly significantly more fit than their ancestor during settling selection (Figure 3A; mean increase = 3%, one-sample t-test, n=20, t=1.633, p=0.12).
evidence: Supported by competition experiments shown in Figure 3A

claim: Snowflake yeast displayed a 5.5% fitness benefit during growth.
source: Snowflake yeast displayed the opposite behavior, possessing a 5.5% fitness benefit during growth (Figure 3A; one-sample t-test, n=20, t=8.374, p<0.0001)
evidence: Supported by competition experiments shown in Figure 3A

claim: Snowflake yeast displayed a 28% fitness advantage during settling selection.
source: and a 28% fitness advantage over their ancestor during settling selection (Figure 3A; one-sample t-test, n=20, t=10.29, p<0.0001).
evidence: Supported by competition experiments shown in Figure 3A

claim: Only 2 out of 20 floc populations had detectably higher fitness than their ancestor during settling selection.
source: Despite floc as an overall treatment group not having higher fitness during settling selection, isolates from 2/20 replicate populations did have detectably higher fitness than their ancestor when competing during settling selection (F20,63=4.528, p<0.0001, multiple comparisons controlled by a Bonferroni correction with overall α=0.05, the same two populations were identified using a Dunnett's test against an ancestor:ancestor control).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of competition experiments

claim: 12 out of 20 snowflake populations significantly increased fitness during settling selection.
source: In contrast, 12/20 snowflake populations significantly increased fitness during settling selection (F20,63=4.89, p<0.0001, multiple comparisons controlled using a Dunnett test against ancestor:ancestor control).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of competition experiments

claim: Overall assortment in floc was relatively low with a mean of 0.06 across five randomly-selected strains.
source: Overall assortment in floc was relatively low (mean of five randomly-selected strains from Figure 3B was 0.06), though there was significant among-strain variation (one-way ANOVA, F4,10=4.159, p=0.008).
evidence: Supported by assortment measurements shown in Figure 3B

claim: Snowflake yeast canonically have an assortment of 1.
source: In contrast, snowflake yeast canonically have an assortment of 1 (when competing two strains, every group is entirely clonal Figure 2—figure supplement 3; Pentz et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citation to Pentz et al., 2020 and Figure 2—figure supplement 3

claim: Floc yeast accumulated more mutations than snowflake yeast, an average of 5 vs 3 mutations per genotype, respectively.
source: Floc yeast accumulated more mutations than snowflake yeast, an average of 5 vs 3 mutations per genotype, respectively (Figure 4A; two-tailed t-test, t=2.49, n=40, p=0.017).
evidence: Supported by whole-genome sequencing data shown in Figure 4A

claim: The overall pattern of mutations observed in snowflake yeast were not distinguishable from drift.
source: The overall pattern of mutations observed in snowflake yeast were not distinguishable from drift, with the number of mutations in each of the four categories being near the mean of the expectation under selective neutrality (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by comparison to null model simulations shown in Figure 4C

claim: The mutations in floc yeast show a strong signature of selection.
source: In contrast, the mutations in floc yeast show a strong signature of selection.
evidence: Supported by comparison to null model showing more missense mutations and fewer synonymous and intergenic mutations than expected

claim: Floc yeast observed more missense mutations than expected based on drift.
source: We observed more missense mutations than expected based on drift (there was a 3% chance of observing at least this many missense mutations in our null model).
evidence: Supported by comparison to null model simulations

claim: Floc yeast observed fewer synonymous mutations than expected based on the null model.
source: Similarly, we observed fewer synonymous mutations and fewer mutations in intergenic regions than expected based on our null model (in both cases, there was a 3% chance of observing this many mutations or fewer in our null model).
evidence: Supported by comparison to null model simulations

claim: Floc yeast observed fewer mutations in intergenic regions than expected based on the null model.
source: Similarly, we observed fewer synonymous mutations and fewer mutations in intergenic regions than expected based on our null model (in both cases, there was a 3% chance of observing this many mutations or fewer in our null model).
evidence: Supported by comparison to null model simulations

claim: Seven parallel missense mutations in GAL2 arose independently in floc.
source: We saw seven parallel missense mutations in GAL2, a transmembrane galactose permease, which may increase the amount of galactose entering the cell.
evidence: Supported by whole-genome sequencing data

claim: Only a single GAL2 mutant arose in snowflake yeast.
source: We saw only a single GAL2 mutant (in contrast to seven arising independently in floc, Supplementary file 2), which is consistent with less growth rate adaptation in snowflake yeast.
evidence: Supported by whole-genome sequencing data

claim: Five parallel missense mutations in FLO1 were observed in floc yeast.
source: Consistent with flocculation itself being under selection, we saw five parallel missense mutations in FLO1, and four in MSN1, a transcriptional activator of another major flocculin gene, FLO11 (Fichtner et al., 2007; van Dyk et al., 2005; Bayly et al., 2005; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by whole-genome sequencing data

claim: Four parallel missense mutations in MSN1 were observed in floc yeast.
source: Consistent with flocculation itself being under selection, we saw five parallel missense mutations in FLO1, and four in MSN1, a transcriptional activator of another major flocculin gene, FLO11 (Fichtner et al., 2007; van Dyk et al., 2005; Bayly et al., 2005; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by whole-genome sequencing data

claim: Floc yeast evolved for eight weeks with only growth rate selection showed a 20.7% increase in fitness during the growth phase.
source: These controls evolved a 20.7% increase in fitness during the growth phase, but evolved a 40% decrease in flocculation efficiency (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by control experiment data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: Floc yeast evolved for eight weeks with only growth rate selection showed a 40% decrease in flocculation efficiency.
source: These controls evolved a 20.7% increase in fitness during the growth phase, but evolved a 40% decrease in flocculation efficiency (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by control experiment data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: Cell-level adaptation to growth on galactose does not drive increased flocculation as a pleiotropic side-effect.
source: We conclude that cell-level adaptation to growth on galactose does not drive increased flocculation as a pleiotropic side-effect.
evidence: Supported by control experiment showing decreased flocculation with growth-only selection

claim: In the clonal life cycle, selection readily acts on mutations that affect cellular growth rate.
source: In the aggregative life cycle, selection readily acts on mutations that affect cellular growth rate (either favoring beneficial mutants or purging those that are deleterious; Figure 5A).
evidence: Inferred from modeling results shown in Figure 5A

claim: In the aggregative life cycle, selection readily acts on mutations that affect cellular growth rate.
source: In the aggregative life cycle, selection readily acts on mutations that affect cellular growth rate (either favoring beneficial mutants or purging those that are deleterious; Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by modeling results shown in Figure 5A

claim: In the clonal life cycle, even mutants that doubled cellular growth rates went extinct approximately 40% of the time.
source: In contrast, the clonal life cycle struggles to capture growth beneficial mutations- even mutants that doubled cellular growth rates went extinct ~40% of the time.
evidence: Supported by modeling results

claim: In the aggregative life cycle, group-beneficial mutations rarely go extinct but cannot be efficiently selected upon.
source: When we examine mutations that increase group survival, we find that while they rarely go extinct in aggregative groups (Figure 5B), neither can they be efficiently selected upon (Figure 5C&D).
evidence: Supported by modeling results shown in Figure 5B, C, and D

claim: In the clonal life cycle, even strongly group-beneficial mutants go extinct far more often than not.
source: In the clonal life cycle, even strongly group-beneficial mutants (e.g., increasing the probability of group survival 10-fold) go extinct far more often than not, as they are extremely susceptible to being lost in the first several rounds of the simulation when they are found in only a small number of groups.
evidence: Supported by modeling results

claim: In the clonal life cycle, group-beneficial mutants that escape being lost by drift rapidly fix in the population.
source: If they escape being lost by drift, however, they rapidly fix in the population (Figure 5C&D).
evidence: Supported by modeling results shown in Figure 5C and D

claim: The clonal life cycle allows selection to act on group-survival beneficial mutations, albeit inefficiently.
source: The clonal life cycle thus allows selection to act, albeit inefficiently, on group-survival beneficial mutations, while the aggregative life cycle is strongly biased in favor of capturing growth-enhancing mutations.
evidence: Supported by modeling results

claim: The aggregative life cycle is strongly biased in favor of capturing growth-enhancing mutations.
source: The clonal life cycle thus allows selection to act, albeit inefficiently, on group-survival beneficial mutations, while the aggregative life cycle is strongly biased in favor of capturing growth-enhancing mutations.
evidence: Supported by modeling results

claim: Only clonally developing snowflake yeast exhibited a shift in Darwinian individuality such that multicellular groups were the primary unit of selection.
source: In this paper, we show that only clonally developing snowflake yeast exhibited a shift in Darwinian individuality (Godfrey-Smith et al., 2013; Rose and Hammerschmidt, 2021), such that multicellular groups were the primary unit of selection, with increased fitness arising mainly via the group-selection phase of the life cycle.
evidence: Supported by competition experiments showing fitness gains primarily during settling selection

claim: Aggregative floc behaved as a social unicellular organism, adapting in both phases of the experiment.
source: Aggregative floc, in contrast, behaved as a social unicellular organism, adapting in both phases of the experiment, but low assortment limited the potential fitness benefits of selection acting on groups.
evidence: Supported by competition experiments and assortment measurements

claim: Low genetic assortment during group formation in floc blunts the impact of group-level selection.
source: Persistent low genetic assortment during group formation presents a challenge to this evolutionary transition, blunting the impact of group-level selection, enabling within-group genetic conflict, and ultimately inhibiting a shift in the level of Darwinian individuality from cells to groups.
evidence: Supported by assortment measurements and fitness competition results

claim: The severity of genetic bottlenecking due to clonal development scales with organismal size.
source: Our model highlights how the severity of genetic bottlenecking due to clonal development scales with organismal size, with larger organisms exacerbating drift.
evidence: Supported by mathematical modeling results

claim: Both snowflake and floc yeast experienced approximately 700 generations over the course of 24 weeks.
source: Thus, over the course of 24 weeks, both snowflake and floc yeast underwent ~700 generations.
evidence: Supported by measurements of doublings per day shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: Snowflake yeast size appeared to plateau after 8-10 weeks of settling selection.
source: Examining one lineage through time, we found that size appeared to plateau after 8–10 weeks of settling selection (Figure 2C), which is consistent with previous work in this model system where aerobic metabolism, and the corresponding reliance on diffused oxygen for growth, strongly inhibits the evolution of increased size (Bozdag et al., 2023; Bozdag et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2C and citations to prior work

claim: Multicellular adaptation requires a positive correlation between group phenotype and underlying cell-level genotype.
source: Multicellular adaptation requires a positive correlation between group phenotype and underlying cell-level genotype; without this, selection acting on groups cannot drive changes in allele frequency (Clarke, 2014; Fletcher and Doebeli, 2009; Pepper and Smuts, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Clarke, 2014; Fletcher and Doebeli, 2009; Pepper and Smuts, 2002

claim: Clonal development has evolved more frequently in aquatic environments.
source: For example, clonal development has evolved more frequently in aquatic environments, while aggregation has evolved more often in terrestrial environments (Bonner, 1998; Fisher et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bonner, 1998; Fisher et al., 2020

claim: Aggregation has evolved more often in terrestrial environments.
source: For example, clonal development has evolved more frequently in aquatic environments, while aggregation has evolved more often in terrestrial environments (Bonner, 1998; Fisher et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bonner, 1998; Fisher et al., 2020

claim: All known transitions to multicellularity occurred in the deep past (>200 MYA).
source: Progress has been limited by the fact that all known transitions to multicellularity occurred in the deep past (>200 MYA Grosberg and Strathmann, 2007; Herron et al., 2009)
evidence: Supported by citations to Grosberg and Strathmann, 2007; Herron et al., 2009

claim: Snowflake yeast were constructed from Saccharomyces cerevisiae strain Y55.
source: These genotypes were created from the same homozygous diploid unicellular ancestor (Saccharomyces cerevisiae strain Y55, accession JRIF00000000)
evidence: Described in the Methods section

claim: Snowflake and floc strains differ only in their mode of cluster formation.
source: so these strains differ only in their mode of cluster formation.
evidence: Described in the Methods section

claim: The selection regime involved 24 hr of batch culture followed by daily selection for rapid sedimentation in liquid media.
source: Our selection regime involved 24 hr of batch culture followed by daily selection for rapid sedimentation in liquid media (Ratcliff et al., 2012).
evidence: Described in the Results section

claim: The selective scheme has previously been shown to promote multicellular adaptation in snowflake yeast.
source: This selective scheme has previously been shown to promote multicellular adaption in snowflake yeast (Ratcliff et al., 2012; Ratcliff et al., 2015; Ratcliff et al., 2013; Bozdag et al., 2023)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: Previous work has led to increases in cluster size of up to 20,000-fold over 600 consecutive rounds of selection.
source: and has led to increases in cluster size of up to 20,000-fold over 600 consecutive rounds of selection (Bozdag et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bozdag et al., 2023

claim: 46% of the putative loss of function mutations in floc are predicted to increase growth rates on galactose.
source: When we query all putative loss of function mutations that arose in our experiment in a genome-wide deletion collection grown on galactose (Giaever et al., 2002), we find that 46% of the mutations in floc are predicted to increase growth rates on this carbon source, in contrast to just 35% in snowflake yeast.
evidence: Supported by comparison to genome-wide deletion collection data

claim: 35% of the putative loss of function mutations in snowflake yeast are predicted to increase growth rates on galactose.
source: When we query all putative loss of function mutations that arose in our experiment in a genome-wide deletion collection grown on galactose (Giaever et al., 2002), we find that 46% of the mutations in floc are predicted to increase growth rates on this carbon source, in contrast to just 35% in snowflake yeast.
evidence: Supported by comparison to genome-wide deletion collection data

claim: Relaxed selection appears to have played a central role in the evolution of larger and more complex genomes within eukaryotes.
source: Indeed, relaxed selection appears to have played a central role in the evolution of larger and more complex genomes within eukaryotes (Lynch and Conery, 2003)
evidence: Supported by citation to Lynch and Conery, 2003

claim: Snowflake yeast evolved to be 20,000 times larger than their ancestor after 400-600 serial transfers.
source: These innovations took 400–600 serial transfers to evolve, and resulted in snowflake yeast that were 20,000 times larger than their ancestor, and 10,000 times more biomechanically tough.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work

claim: Snowflake yeast evolved to be 10,000 times more biomechanically tough after 400-600 serial transfers.
source: These innovations took 400–600 serial transfers to evolve, and resulted in snowflake yeast that were 20,000 times larger than their ancestor, and 10,000 times more biomechanically tough.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work

claim: Evolving macroscopic size appears somewhat trivial for floc, likely due to the relative ease of increasing the strength of cell-cell adhesion.
source: In contrast, evolving macroscopic size (Figure 2F) appears somewhat trivial for floc, likely due the relative ease and efficacy of increasing the strength of cell-cell adhesion.
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations and comparison to snowflake yeast

claim: Clonal multicellular development provides the foundation upon which sustained multicellular adaptation may ultimately drive the evolution of dramatically increased multicellular complexity.
source: There is an emerging consensus that clonal multicellular development provides the foundation upon which sustained multicellular adaptation may ultimately drive the evolution of dramatically increased multicellular complexity.
evidence: Supported by citations to phylogenetic inference, theory, and experimental evolution

claim: Most lineages of aggregative multicellularity are terrestrial.
source: To this latter point, most lineages of aggregative multicellularity are terrestrial (Bonner, 1998; Fisher et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citations to Bonner, 1998; Fisher et al., 2020

claim: Snowflake yeast must resolve fundamental biophysical challenges before they can form large groups.
source: Snowflake yeast must resolve fundamental biophysical challenges before they can form large groups, evolving larger size via three distinct biophysical mechanisms: reducing cellular density within clusters to limit cell-cell jamming, increasing the size and strength of the bonds connecting mother and daughter cells, and evolving branch entanglement so that group fracture requires breaking many cellular bonds, not just one (Bozdag et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bozdag et al., 2023

claim: Snowflake yeast evolve larger size via three distinct biophysical mechanisms: reducing cellular density, increasing bond size and strength, and evolving branch entanglement.
source: evolving larger size via three distinct biophysical mechanisms: reducing cellular density within clusters to limit cell-cell jamming, increasing the size and strength of the bonds connecting mother and daughter cells, and evolving branch entanglement so that group fracture requires breaking many cellular bonds, not just one (Bozdag et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bozdag et al., 2023

claim: In a rare beneficial mutant scenario, if the proportion of mutant cells is small compared to the number of groups, each group would contain only a single mutant cell in an idealized aggregative development.
source: Such a scenario could arise in a population without preferential assortment (i.e. an idealized form of aggregative development) if the proportion of mutant cells is small in comparison to the number of groups.
evidence: Described in the mathematical modeling section

claim: When groups are highly assorted (e.g. clonal development), a rare beneficial mutant and all of its descendants will be represented in a small number of groups.
source: In contrast, when groups are highly assorted (e.g. clonal development), the initially rare mutant and all of its descendants will be represented in a small number of groups, reducing k by a factor that corresponds to mean group size.
evidence: Described in the mathematical modeling section

claim: If a mutant arises at the beginning of the growth phase and the population grows 100-fold, resulting in 100 mutant cells with an average group size of 50 cells and 1% survival, the probability that the mutant lineage goes extinct in a clonally developing population is 98%.
source: To get a sense of this effect, suppose a mutant arises at the beginning of the growth phase. The population then grows 100-fold, resulting in 100 mutant cells. Assuming the average size of a group is 50 cells, then if 1% of the population survives settling selection, the probability that the mutant lineage goes extinct in a population that develops clonally is 98%, while it is just 36.4% for a population developing aggregatively.
evidence: Calculated from mathematical model

claim: If a mutant arises at the beginning of the growth phase and the population grows 100-fold, resulting in 100 mutant cells with an average group size of 50 cells and 1% survival, the probability that the mutant lineage goes extinct in an aggregatively developing population is 36.4%.
source: To get a sense of this effect, suppose a mutant arises at the beginning of the growth phase. The population then grows 100-fold, resulting in 100 mutant cells. Assuming the average size of a group is 50 cells, then if 1% of the population survives settling selection, the probability that the mutant lineage goes extinct in a population that develops clonally is 98%, while it is just 36.4% for a population developing aggregatively.
evidence: Calculated from mathematical model

claim: 88% of the beneficial mutants within the clonal lineages went extinct in the model where sg = 10.
source: Note that 88% of the beneficial mutants within the clonal lineages went extinct in D.
evidence: Stated in the caption of Figure 5

claim: Fitness in the experiment depends on growth rate during the 24 hr of batch culture and survival during the subsequent settling selection step.
source: Fitness in our experiment depends on growth rate during the 24 hr of batch culture when the population is competing for resources, and survival during the subsequent settling selection step (Pentz et al., 2020; Ratcliff et al., 2012; Conlin and Ratcliff, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: The main way in which a lineage can increase survival during settling selection is through changes in the phenotype of multicellular groups.
source: In contrast, the main way in which a lineage can increase survival during settling selection is through changes in the phenotype of multicellular groups (i.e. increasing their size, packing density, or hydrodynamic profile Ratcliff et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ratcliff et al., 2013
